draft.title: Asymmetric information
card: Asymmetric information is when one side of a deal knows more than the other. The seller usually knows more, but sometimes the buyer does.
The side with less information may pay too much, buy a poor product or avoid the deal. Prices then no longer reflect the true cost or benefit of the good.
Example: a person selling a used car knows its faults. The buyer cannot easily check them, so the buyer may offer a low price even for a good car.
This can lead to a market failure. Some good-quality sellers may leave the market, and the amount traded is not the best one for society.
draft.remember: Asymmetric information means one side knows more, so the market can give poor results.

opts: A mechanic knows a car's faults but the buyer does not
Two firms both know the price of steel and trade it
A shop and its customers both read the same price tag
A buyer and a seller each check a car and agree on a fault
a.why: The mechanic knows more about the car than the buyer, so the two sides hold different information. In the other options both sides know the same things, so there is no gap.
a.clue: Look for the deal where one side knows more.

b.q: Dev wants to buy a used car in Geelong. He cannot check its history, so he offers a low price even for a good car. Why does this offer cause a poor market result?
opts: Sellers of good cars may leave, so fewer good cars are sold
Sellers of good cars will lift their prices to match his offer
Buyers will pay more, as they know the cars are all faulty
The market will trade more good cars than society needs
b.why: When buyers cannot tell good cars from bad, they offer low prices, and sellers of good cars may leave the market. The market then trades fewer good cars than is best. Higher prices do not follow, because buyers are offering less.
b.clue: Think about what a seller of a good car does when offers are low.
